title: Saline-Free Surgical Preparation of Adult Drosophila for Brain Imaging
author: Zhu, Khorbtli, et al.
materials: This saline-free approach minimizes tissue damage, maintains physiological consistency, and enhances animal viability, enabling reliable, chronic in vivo observations. Compared with prior complex laser-based approaches,5,6 this simplified manual preparation is cost-effective and suitable for wider adoption across the Drosophila research community. Furthermore, this protocol may also be extended to long-term brain imaging in other insect species with minimal modifications.

This section outlines the steps for mounting a fly to a rigid holder to minimize motion artifacts during surgery or imaging while ensuring the animal remains awake and healthy.1.Install an acrylic fly holder on the metal bar using a screw (Figure 1C), then clamp the bar to the multi-axis stage of the tethering station (Figure 1A).2.Anesthetize selected flies by placing the vial on ice for 1 min.Note: We exclusively use female flies for imaging, though this surgical protocol applies to both sexes. Male flies have a higher post-surgical mortality rate due to their smaller size.3.Transfer an anesthetized fly onto the cooled aluminum surface (∼4°C) of the thermoelectric cooling block (Figure 2A).Figure 2Fly mounting procedure(A) The tethering station is placed under a stereoscope for fly mounting. The inset shows a zoomed-in view of the installed fly holder and the cooling block.(B) Top view of the fly positioned on the cooling surface with its head supported by the washer (yellow arrow).(C) A drop of UV glue applied to the pin (yellow arrow).(D) Top view of the fly with its thorax fixed to the pin (yellow arrow).(E) The fly’s head is glued to its thorax from both sides (yellow arrows). Scale bars: 1 mm in B–E.4.Using dull forceps (Dumont AA), gently adjust the fly’s orientation under the stereoscope (Ivesta 3) so that the fly’s ventral side faces the aluminum block (Figure 2B).Note: Position the fly's proboscis against a flat washer (Size M2, 5 mm outer diameter) on the aluminum block. This helps maintain the fly's natural standing posture.5.Apply approximately 1 μL of UV-curable epoxy (NOA 81; Figure 1D left) to the middle point of the pin on the acrylic fly holder. Use the multi-axis stage to move the acrylic fly holder directly above the fly’s thorax (Figure 2C).Note: Use the insect pin with a bent tip to dip and transfer the epoxy (Figure 1E left).Note: Alternatively, the glue can be applied to the pin before positioning the fly.6.Lower the holder and bring the pin into contact with the dorsal side of the fly’s thorax. Let the epoxy spread over the posterior thorax cuticle.7.Cure the epoxy with the UV wand (Norland Inc.) for 5 s to create a stable bond (Figure 2D).CRITICAL: UV exposure time and distance must be carefully calibrated. In our setup, we use 365/385 nm wavelengths for 5 s with the UV wand tip approximately 2 cm away from the fly. If using a different UV wand, adjust the distance between the UV wand and the fly to prevent overheating (which can be lethal) or incomplete solidification of the glue.8.To stabilize the head, apply approximately 0.5 μL of UV epoxy onto each side of the fly’s head to firmly secure the head to the thorax (Figure 2E). Cure the glue with UV light. Inadequate stabilization can result in head detachment or severe z-axis motion during imaging.CRITICAL: For optimal access to the target neuron population, the head orientation should be fine-tuned with the micromanipulator. Moving the fly’s body toward or away from the washer changes the head pitch angle. For imaging anterior brain regions, fix the head as shown in Figure 2D; for imaging posterior structures such as Kenyon cells, fix the head as shown in Figure 2B.Note: To achieve a stable head–thorax bond, the adhesive typically covers the posterior half of both eyes. Because the cured UV epoxy is transparent to visible light, flies still display normal behavioral responses to light under our experimental conditions. However, for experiments requiring precise visual stimulation or fine measurements of visual responses, partial eye coverage may be a concern. In such cases, we recommend securing the posterior side of the head instead so that the eyes remain fully unobstructed.9.After removing flies from the tethering station, allow flies to recover at 22–25°C for 1 min before the surgery. Ensure the head-fixed fly is fully awake and active on the holder.Note: See Methods video S1 for the full mounting procedure.
More detailed designs of the mounting platform and Drosophila lines are available upon request from the lead contact.

steps.title: Assemble tethering station and gather tools
steps.instruction: Build the custom tethering station, attach the acrylic fly holder to a metal bar, install the UV‑curable epoxy, UV wand, and surgical tools (Minutien pins with nickel‑plated holder, tungsten needle with Moria holder, Dumont #5SF and AA forceps) as described in the supplemental assembly guide.

steps.title: Prepare flies for mounting
steps.instruction: Cross the chosen GAL4 line with the fluorescent reporter, raise flies on standard cornmeal agar at 25 °C, 50 % RH, 12 h light/dark. Select healthy female (or male) flies that are 5–8 days old after eclosion for the procedure.

steps.title: Mount fly to acrylic holder
steps.instruction: Secure the fly to the holder while keeping it awake and oriented correctly.

substeps.instruction: Install the acrylic holder on the metal bar with a screw and clamp the bar to the multi‑axis stage of the tethering station.
Place the fly vial on ice for 1 min to anesthetize the flies (use only females for best survival).
Transfer an anesthetized fly onto the cooled aluminum surface of the thermoelectric block (~4 °C).
Using Dumont AA dull forceps, adjust the fly so its ventral side faces the block and its proboscis rests against a 5 mm outer‑diameter M2 washer.
Apply ~1 µL of UV‑curable epoxy NOA 81 to the middle of the insect pin on the holder (dip the bent‑tip pin into the epoxy).
Lower the holder so the pin contacts the dorsal thorax; let the epoxy spread over the posterior thorax cuticle.
Cure the epoxy with the UV wand (365/385 nm) for 5 s at ~2 cm distance (adjust if using a different wand).
Apply ~0.5 µL of NOA 81 epoxy to each side of the head to bond head to thorax; cure with UV light (same settings).
Fine‑tune head pitch with the micromanipulator for the target brain region (anterior or posterior).
Allow the mounted fly to recover at 22–25 °C for 1 min; ensure it is fully awake before proceeding.

steps.title: Perform saline‑free brain surgery
steps.instruction: Expose the brain and create a sealed optical window without using saline.

substeps.instruction: Move the holder with the mounted fly under the stereoscope.
Maintain ambient humidity at 35–60 % using a desktop humidifier; keep the washer and cooling block dry with a Kimwipe.
Shorten or remove all bristles over the target head area with sharp Dumont #5SF forceps.
Using the 1 µm‑tip tungsten needle, poke a series of small holes around the intended window perimeter (window diameter ≈0.3–0.4 mm); avoid deep penetration.
Carefully peel off the perforated cuticle with sharp forceps to expose the brain.
Gently skim away air sacs (white net‑like) and fat tissue (opaque round) without scraping the brain surface.
Apply ~1 µL of UV‑curable epoxy NOA 68 to seal the cuticle opening; cure for 5 s with the UV wand.

If a water‑immersion objective will be used, place a ~1 mm × 0.5 mm piece of #0 coverslip onto the sealed window: cure the first NOA 68 layer, add a second NOA 68 layer, then gently lay the coverslip (do not press into uncured epoxy).
If needed, add extra NOA 68 epoxy around the neck to raise the glue height and keep the antennae clear of the coverslip; cure the added epoxy.

steps.title: Image brain through transparent window
steps.instruction: Acquire longitudinal fluorescence images using the appropriate microscope configuration.

substeps.instruction: Place the acrylic holder on the microscope stage and position under the fluorescence (or two‑photon) microscope.
Apply ~2 µL of distilled water to the tip of the water‑immersion objective.
Lower the objective until the water droplet contacts the coverslip over the fly’s head.
Perform imaging:
• For voltage imaging: use a 1.0 NA 20× XLUMPlanFLN objective, 475 nm LED (≈5 mW mm⁻²), 474/27 nm excitation filter, 488 nm dichroic, 520/35 nm emission filter; acquire at 1002 Hz with 2 × 2 binning.
• For calcium imaging: use a two‑photon system with 920 nm laser, same objective, acquire at 10 Hz (380 × 252 px) with 20 % PMT gain; illumination ≈10 mW mm⁻².
Maintain consistent ROI selection across days for longitudinal studies.

steps.title: Release fly and post‑imaging care
steps.instruction: Detach the fly from the holder and return it to food, monitoring for glue residue.

substeps.instruction: Under the stereoscope, use the tip of dull forceps to push the coverslip and break the cured epoxy securing the thorax pin.
Gently grasp the fly by its wings with the forceps and transfer it to a fresh food vial.
Check for residual external glue (especially head‑thorax) that may cause the fly to stick to the vial wall; remove any stuck flies promptly.

For subsequent sessions, either remount the fly using the initial mounting procedure or keep it on the holder and feed it three times daily with 100 mM sucrose solution applied to the proboscis via micropipette or Kimwipe.

steps.title: Maintain environmental conditions and troubleshoot
steps.instruction: Ensure humidity, UV curing, and glue application are within optimal ranges to prevent common problems.

substeps.instruction: Keep relative humidity between 35 % and 60 % (ideally 35–50 %); use a humidifier for low humidity and reduce output or raise block temperature if condensation appears.
Before UV curing, verify wand distance (~2 cm) and exposure time (5 s); adjust if flies overheat or epoxy remains uncured.
If the fly detaches, confirm full curing of thorax‑pin bond and head‑thorax epoxy (increase cure time slightly if needed).
To avoid epoxy seeping into the brain, apply NOA 68 only along the cuticle rim and cure the first layer before adding the coverslip.
If excessive z‑motion occurs, add a small amount of UV epoxy to the dorsal neck region and ensure the holder is firmly clamped and the stage is vibration‑free.
